items.title: 68239_Ram Ramirez oral history interview
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] ...the mother was Cherokee or something... [INTERVIEWEE] Oh yeah! It was all part of it.

ctx.x: But if you read history, all in that... Especially in the South at least, the Blacks and Indians intermarried extensively. Well, you know lots of Jazz musicians who are part Indian; you know, the mother was Cherokee or something. Now, it must be somewhere in there contributions from the Indians to that music. I mean, just as we know that in New Orleans, say, that the Black music is influenced by European music because they were exposed to it a lot, the Indian contribution is in there somewhere -- but we don't…

Oh yeah! It was all part of it. Especially in the old days with movies, when so-called the railroad was... In the old films, you know, the Indians were waiting at the so-called... The actors who were made up as Indians were waiting to attack the White settlers. All of a sudden you hear, 'Whoo-ooo,' BOOM-BOOM-BOOM-BOOM... And I would say it was kind of Oriental, too, you know, in character. But that was their sound; it comes from the drums, from their drums. Although their rhythmic patterns were different. But…
